title: Phrasal Verb Farm
intro: Travel, work, relationships and money: match each everyday phrasal verb to its meaning.

A2.right: arrive and register at a hotel or airport
A2.why: At the hotel desk or airport counter you “check in” first: you register your arrival.

A2.right: enter a bus, train or plane
A2.why: We “get on” buses, trains and planes, but we “get in” a car or taxi.
“He turned up at ten”: used when someone arrives, often late or without warning.

A2.right: give a finished piece of work to someone
A2.why: You “hand in” a form or a report: you give it to the person who asked for it.
Your alarm rings and you wake up; then you get up and leave your bed.
A couple “breaks up” when the relationship ends, like Spanish “romper”.
You borrowed it, so you pay it back: Spanish “devolver” the money.

A2.right: keep money to buy something later
A2.why: “Up” suggests adding more and more: you save up for a holiday or a car.

A2.right: leave a bus, train or plane
A2.why: The opposite of “get on”: you get off the train at Valencia Nord.
You look for your keys (try to find them), but you look at a picture.

A2.right: complete a form with your details
A2.why: At the doctor's you fill in a form: you write your details in the spaces.
Spanish “salir”: on Friday night we go out for tapas.

B1.why: Friends “fall out” after an argument; the opposite is “make up”.
You look up, as at someone taller: you admire them.

B1.right: hire someone, or accept a responsibility
B1.why: A company takes on new staff, and you can take on extra work.
When a colleague is ill, you fill in for them: Spanish “sustituir”.
The cowboys set off at dawn: they began the journey.
The opposite of “check in”: you pay the bill and leave the hotel.
“We've run out of milk” = there's none left. Spanish “quedarse sin”.

B1.right: save money for a particular purpose
B1.why: You put some money aside each month, for a holiday for example.

B1.right: have a good relationship with someone
B1.why: “I get on well with my neighbours”: we have a friendly relationship.
“I'll pick you up at the station”: Spanish “recoger”.
In 1854 John Snow found out that dirty water spread cholera: he discovered it.
The doctor told him to give up smoking: Spanish “dejar de”.

B2.why: The opposite of “look up to”: you think you are better than them.
You arrive late, so you buy the coffees to make up for it: you compensate.

B2.right: dismiss employees due to lack of work
B2.why: Workers are laid off when there isn't enough work, not because they did something wrong.
Doctors carry out operations and scientists carry out experiments: they do them.
Traffic held us up: it delayed us. Outlaws also “held up” stagecoaches to rob them.

B2.right: fail to pay or finish on time
B2.why: If you get behind with the rent, the payments are late and keep piling up.

B2.right: spend a lot of money on something special
B2.why: Like money splashing everywhere: you spend generously on a treat.
Everyone chips in a few euros for a colleague's present.
She turned down the job in Madrid: she said no to it.
At a Valencia flea market I came across an old map: I found it without looking.
He set up a small bakery in Ruzafa: he started a business.

B2.right: take control of a company or job
B2.why: When the old sheriff retired, his deputy took over.

C1.right: begin to feel strongly attracted to someone
C1.why: You fall for someone fast, as if falling. It can also mean being tricked by a lie.

C1.right: become friends again after a serious quarrel
C1.why: Like patching a hole in your clothes: you repair a friendship after a quarrel.

C1.right: send work to be done by someone outside the company
C1.why: The company farms out its accounts: another firm does that work for it.

C1.right: expand into a new area of business
C1.why: Like a tree growing new branches: the business grows into new areas.

C1.right: cost someone a large amount of money
C1.why: Informal: “That car set me back 20,000 euros” = it cost me that much.

C1.right: rescue a person or company from financial trouble
C1.why: Sailors bail water out of a sinking boat; governments bail out failing banks.

C1.right: change direction suddenly, leaving the intended path
C1.why: The wagon veered off the trail: it suddenly changed direction.

C1.right: quickly form a good relationship with someone
C1.why: Two people hit it off when they like each other immediately.

C1.right: solve small technical or practical problems before something starts
C1.why: Like ironing the creases out of a shirt: you smooth out the problems.

C1.right: get rid of someone with an excuse or an inferior substitute
C1.why: The shop fobbed me off with a cheap replacement to make me go away.

C1.right: slowly become less close over time
C1.why: Like two boats on the sea: no argument, the friends just grow distant.

C1.right: earn a lot of money easily
C1.why: Like raking up leaves: the money comes in by the pile.
